0.html:
Documentation for the H system — an event-sourced personal-computing environment.

The first thing documented here is Woodr — Woopy's drawing — the small declarative language Woopy speaks to draw explanations directly on your screen while it talks. It began as a handful of annotation tags and grew, over one intense session, into a real compositional language: relational geometry, iteration, macros, conditionals, constraint solving, and a library that grows itself.

2.html: Woodr lets you coin a construction once and reuse it — the equivalent of functions. This is the feature that turns a fixed vocabulary into a language that can grow.
2.text:
Woodr lets you coin a construction once and reuse it — the equivalent of functions.
This is the feature that turns a fixed vocabulary into a language that can grow.
2.title: Abstraction

3.html:
[DEF:NAME:param1,param2,…]
  …body using $param1, $param2 …
[ENDDEF]

The body is ordinary Woodr. Parameters are written $name and substituted at each use.
3.text:

3.title: [DEF] … [ENDDEF]

4.html:
[USE:NAME:arg1,arg2,…]

Expands the macro body inline with the arguments substituted. Arguments are typically @point references or numbers.
4.title: [USE]

6.html:
Notice both uses define a local point called m. Woodr auto-namespaces each macro's own defined names per call, so they never clash — the first USE becomes u1_m, the second u2_m, transparently. You can USE the same macro as many times as you like.

A macro that draws a repeated motif (a graph node, a molecule, a UML box) plus iteration is powerful: [REPEAT] the anchor points, then [USE] the motif at each one.

7.html: A one-off [DEF] lives for a single reply. To keep a good construction forever, Woopy can save it to the library with draw_lib_add — after which it's fetchable by name on any future turn. That's how Woodr's vocabulary grows over time.

A one-off [DEF] lives for a single reply. To keep a good construction forever, Woopy
can save it to the library with draw_lib_add — after which it's
fetchable by name on any future turn. That's how Woodr's vocabulary grows over time.
7.title: Growing the library

8.html: Woodr is unusual among drawing languages: it has time. A Woodr program isn't rendered all at once — it plays, in step with what Woopy is saying.
8.text:
Woodr is unusual among drawing languages: it has time. A Woodr program isn't rendered
all at once — it plays, in step with what Woopy is saying.
8.title: Choreography

9.html:
Woopy's reply streams sentence by sentence, and each sentence's marks are revealed the moment that sentence is spoken. So you place a tag right where you say the words for it:

First, here's the circle. [CIRCLE:O:960,540,300]
Now pick a point on top. [PT:B:on O 90][POINT:@B:B]

The circle appears as Woopy says "here's the circle"; B appears as it says "on top". Marks accumulate as the explanation builds.

[PAUSE:800]Hold ~0.8 s before the next beat
[CLEAR]Wipe the current marks — start a fresh step (spotlight one thing at a time)
[BEAT]Force a new beat inside a single sentence

Step one — click here. [POINT:@save:save] [PAUSE:600]
[CLEAR] Step two — now the menu opens. [POINT:@menu:menu]

13.html: By default Woodr draws in a single blue accent. [COLOR] changes the pen: every mark drawn after it takes that color, until the next [COLOR] — or the turn / a [CLEAR] resets it to blue.

13.title: Color

14.html:
[COLOR:name]

It's a state change, not a drawn mark — think of it as picking up a differently colored pen. Set it at the start of the sentence whose marks it applies to.

[COLOR:green]the average line [LINE:@A,@C]
[COLOR:red]and the tangent [LINE:@P,@Q]

15.html:
Colors can be named by meaning or by hue — both map to bright, overlay-friendly values that read on light and dark screens.

SemanticHue aliases
goodgreen, ok, go
badred, danger, error, wrong
warnamber, yellow, warning
infocyan, teal
accent (default)blue
—orange, purple, pink, white

16.html:
Two jobs:

  1. Distinguish parts. A diagram with a curve, a secant, and a tangent all in one blue is hard to read. Blue curve, green secant, red tangent separates them instantly.
  2. Carry meaning. good/green vs bad/red vs warn/amber lets a mark mean something before the label is even read.

[CHECK] (green ✓) and [CROSS] (red ✗) keep their intrinsic colors regardless of the pen — they're inherently semantic.

17.html:
Where [COLOR] sets one pen, [THEME:name] picks a named preset for everything after it — the flat, deterministic version of Penrose's content/cosmetics split (no separate style language, just a bag of defaults).

[THEME:blueprint]   the whole figure now draws in the blueprint pen
ThemePen
chalksoft white
blueprintblue
sunsetorange
forestgreen
grapepurple

18.title: Conditionals

19.html:
[IF:condition] …kept when true… [ELSE] …kept when false… [ENDIF]

The [ELSE] branch is optional. Conditionals are evaluated after macro parameters and loop indices are filled in, so by the time a condition is checked both sides are numbers.

20.html: Supported operators: >, <, >=, <=, ==, !=, and % (modulo) inside the arithmetic. Examples: $val > 50, i % 2 == 0, 3 >= 2.
20.text:
Supported operators: >, <, >=, <=, ==, !=, and % (modulo) inside the

20.title: Comparisons

21.html:
The natural home for [IF] is a [DEF] whose output depends on a parameter:

[DEF:node:val,x,y]
  [ELLIPSE:$x,$y,34,34:]
  [TEXT:$x,$y:$val]
  [IF:$val >= 50][CHECK:$x,$y][ELSE][CROSS:$x,$y][ENDIF]
[ENDDEF]

[USE:node:70,600,300]     // draws a ✓ (70 ≥ 50)
[USE:node:20,900,300]     // draws a ✗ (20 < 50)

23.html: These are the advanced relational forms — points defined by solving a geometric constraint. Like the rest of the kernel, you state the relationship and the renderer computes the exact pixel. They're written the same way: [PT:NAME:EXPR].
23.text:
These are the advanced relational forms — points defined by solving a geometric

23.title: Constraints

24.html:
[PT:X:intersect A B C D]

The point where line A–B crosses line C–D. (Returns nothing if the lines are parallel.) Great for diagonals, cevians, or where a construction line meets an axis.
24.text:
[PT:X:intersect A B C D]

parallel.) Great for diagonals, cevians, or where a construction line meets an axis.
24.title: intersect

25.html:
[PT:F:foot P A B]

The foot of the perpendicular from P onto line A–B — i.e. the projection of P onto that line. Useful for altitudes, dropping a value to an axis, or a right-angle construction.
25.text:

26.html:
[PT:P2:rotate P C deg]

P rotated around centre C by deg degrees. Compose it with iteration to spin a motif around a point.

27.html:
[PT:O:circumcenter A B C]

The centre of the unique circle passing through A, B, and C. Pair it with a [CIRCLE] to draw that circumscribed circle exactly.

28.html:
[PT:T:tangent P O side]     // side = +1 or -1 (the two tangent points)

The point on circle O where a line from the external point P just touches the circle. The line P→T is guaranteed perpendicular to the radius O→T — a true tangent. There are two; side picks which.

29.html: Constraint-defined points are the difference between a diagram that looks roughly right and one that is provably correct. An altitude drawn with foot really is perpendicular; a tangent drawn with tangent really does touch. The author never computes any of it.
29.text:
Constraint-defined points are the difference between a diagram that looks roughly right

tangent drawn with tangent really does touch. The author never computes any of it.
29.title: Why this matters

30.html: For a graph, a curve, or anything with a tangent, Woodr has a real function object. You give a formula; the renderer samples it, draws the exact curve, and lets you place points on it and draw tangents that genuinely touch it. No hand-picked points, no eyeballing.

30.title: Functions & curves

31.html:
[PLOT:NAME:formula:x0,x1,bx,by,bw,bh:label]

Draws the function formula (in x) sampled over the domain [x0, x1], mapped into the screen box (bx, by, bw, bh) — and registers it under NAME. The y-axis is flipped so larger values are higher on screen.

[PLOT:f:x^2:-3,3,700,300,520,340:y = x²]

32.html:
The evaluator understands: + - * / % ^, parentheses, unary minus, the constants pi and e, and the functions sin cos tan asin acos atan sqrt abs exp ln log.

sin(x)        0.5*x^2 - 2       exp(-x^2)       sqrt(x)        3*sin(2*x)+1

33.html:
[PT:P:onplot NAME xval]

Resolves to the point on the plotted curve at x = xval, in screen pixels. Because it uses the same function and mapping as the drawn curve, the point is guaranteed to sit on it.

[PLOT:f:x^2:-3,3,700,300,520,340:y=x²]
[PT:C:onplot f 1][POINT:@C:here]

34.html:
[PT:L:tanpoint NAME xval -120]
[PT:R:tanpoint NAME xval 120]
[LINE:@L,@R]

tanpoint NAME x dpx is a point dpx screen-pixels sideways from the contact point, along the tangent to the curve at x. The renderer computes the slope, so the line through two tanpoints is a real tangent — it touches the curve at x and nowhere near it crosses by accident.

34.title: A true tangent — tanpoint

35.html:
[PLOT:f:0.6*x^2 - 0.1*x^3:0,5,300,200,900,500:the drive]
[PT:A:onplot f 0][PT:B:onplot f 5]
[COLOR:green][LINE:@A,@B:average]
[PT:L:tanpoint f 3 -140][PT:R:tanpoint f 3 140]
[COLOR:red][LINE:@L,@R:tangent] [PT:C:onplot f 3][POINT:@C:this moment]

The average (secant) is green, the tangent is red and actually touches the curve at the marked moment — the whole point of the theorem, drawn exactly.

This is the right tool for derivatives, tangents, the Mean Value Theorem, and integrals — anything where a point must lie on a curve or a line must be tangent to it.

36.html: Woodr is a set of tags interleaved with what Woopy says. Tags are never spoken — only the text outside tags is read aloud. Everything renders on a transparent overlay on the active monitor, in pixels: x grows right (0..W), y grows down (0..H).

36.title: Getting started

37.html:
1. A mark — something drawn: a point, line, circle, polygon, label, …
  2. A named point — [PT:NAME:…] binds a coordinate to a name.
  3. A reference — @NAME drops that point's coordinates wherever a coordinate goes.

A named point — [PT:NAME:…] binds a coordinate to a name.
A reference — @NAME drops that point's coordinates wherever a coordinate goes.
37.title: The three things you need

38.html:
[PT:A:400,600][PT:B:900,600][PT:C:650,300]
[POLY:@A;@B;@C:triangle]

That defines three points and draws a triangle through them. Note you named each point once — you never re-typed 400,600. That alone removes a whole class of mistakes (connecting the wrong corners, mismatched coordinates).

38.title: Your first diagram

39.html:
Instead of eyeballing where C goes, put it on a circle:

[CIRCLE:O:650,500,200]      // circle named O
[PT:A:on O 200][PT:B:on O 340][PT:C:on O 90]
[POLY:@A;@B;@C:] [POINT:@C:top]

Now C is guaranteed to sit on the circle. This is the heart of Woodr — see Points & the kernel →.

Woopy places each mark as it says the words for it — so tags are written right where they belong in the narration. See Choreography.

39.title: Make it exact

40.html:
Woodr — Woopy's drawing — is the language Woopy uses to draw on your screen while it explains something out loud. You don't write Woodr; Woopy speaks it. But it is a real language, with the properties that make one:

  • Composition — marks are built from named points, and points are defined by their relationship to other points. Meaning builds from smaller meaning.
  • Naming / binding — [PT:NAME:…] binds a name; @NAME references it.
  • An evaluator — the kernel resolver parses Woodr, solves the relationships, and compiles down to exact pixels.
  • Iteration & abstraction — [REPEAT] and [DEF]/[USE] — loops and functions.
  • A growing library — verified constructions Woopy can fetch and even add to.
40.text:

40.title: Woodr

41.html:
The hard part of drawing a diagram is the geometry — where does a triangle's vertex land so it sits exactly on a circle? A language model is bad at that arithmetic and tends to eyeball it a few pixels off. Woodr removes the problem: you state the relationship and the renderer computes the exact pixel.

[CIRCLE:O:960,540,300]      // a circle named O
[PT:B:on O 90]              // B is EXACTLY on O at the top — not "about (960,240)"

Because B is defined as "on the circle at the top", it can never drift. Precision is structural, not a thing the author has to get right.

42.html:
1. It's embedded in speech. Woodr is woven through natural-language narration, emitted by an LLM in real time. It isn't written to a file — it's spoken, tag by tag, as Woopy talks.
  2. It has time. Choreography — beats, pauses, reveals — means a Woodr program doesn't just render, it plays, in step with the words.

42.title: Two unusual properties

43.html:
A full proof of Thales' theorem, drawn exactly, without typing a single coordinate twice:

[CIRCLE:O:960,540,300]
[PT:A:on O 180][PT:B:on O 90][PT:C:on O 0]
[LINE:@A,@C] [POLY:@A;@B;@C:] [RIGHTANGLE:@B,@A,@C]
[POINT:@A:A][POINT:@B:B][POINT:@C:C][POINT:@O:O]

Every point is exact, the right angle is snug in the corner, and the whole thing fades after Woopy finishes explaining it.

Continue to Getting started →.

43.title: What a Woodr program looks like

44.html: When a figure needs many points in a pattern — a polygon's vertices, a grid, tick marks, orbiting dots — you don't list them by hand. Woodr has a loop.
44.text:

44.title: Iteration

45.html:
[REPEAT:NAME:count:pointExpr]

Defines NAME0, NAME1, … NAME(count-1). Inside pointExpr, the loop index i (0-based) is available in any arithmetic.

[CIRCLE:O:960,540,300]
[REPEAT:V:6:on O 60*i]      // V0..V5 at 0°, 60°, 120°, …, 300°

The little arithmetic evaluator supports + - * / % and parentheses — so 60*i, i/5, 90 + i*45, i%2 all work.

49.html: The kernel is the small core of Woodr that everything else is built on: named, relationally-defined points. This is where Woodr's precision comes from — you describe a point by its relationship to other things, and the renderer computes the exact pixel.

52.html:
A circle can be named so points can sit on it:

[CIRCLE:O:960,540,300:label]     // centre (960,540), radius 300
[CIRCLE:O:@Center,300]           // centre is a named point

Naming a circle both draws it and registers it for on. Here every vertex is placed by relationship — on O deg — so the right angle is exact (Thales' theorem):

FormMeaning
on O degExactly on circle O at an angle (0 = right, 90 = top, 180 = left, 270 = bottom)
mid A BMidpoint of A and B
along A B tA fraction t (0..1) of the way from A to B
polar A r degDistance r from A at an angle
offset A dx dyA shifted by (dx, dy)

More advanced constraints — intersect, foot, rotate, circumcenter, tangent — extend this same grammar.

54.html: For a circle centred at (cx, cy) with radius r, the point at angle θ is (cx + r·cosθ, cy − r·sinθ) (the minus because y grows downward). A model asked to compute that will often land a few pixels off, so a triangle's vertex floats near the circle instead of on it. By writing on O 90, the renderer does the trig — the vertex touches the arc, every time.

55.html:
[RIGHTANGLE:@corner,@a,@b]

Draws a small square snug in the corner at @corner, between the directions to @a and @b. The renderer computes the corner geometry, so it's always tucked in the angle — not floating nearby.

56.html: The kernel is a compile pass. [PT], [CIRCLE], [RIGHTANGLE], and the constructs on the next pages are all resolved down to the plain marks — [ELLIPSE], [POLY], [LINE], … — before anything is drawn. So the kernel adds power without needing any new rendering: it's a language on top of the marks.

57.html: The kernel builds most figures directly. For named or complex constructions — a theorem diagram, a set of axes, a bell curve, a tree — Woodr has a searchable library of verified recipes, fetched only when needed.
57.text:
The kernel builds most figures directly. For named or complex
constructions — a theorem diagram, a set of axes, a bell curve, a tree — Woodr has a
searchable library of verified recipes, fetched only when needed.
57.title: The library

58.html:
• Kernel (always available): relational points, marks, iteration, macros — the fast path. A circle, a triangle, an arrow: just draw it.
  • Library (fetched): higher-level constructions. Fetching is a tool round-trip, so it's reserved for figures worth it — never for a basic shape.

This split keeps the common case instant while letting the library scale without bloating what Woopy carries in its head.

59.html:
Woopy searches by topic and gets back a recipe in Woodr to adapt:

draw_lib("thales theorem")
draw_lib("normal distribution")
draw_lib("binary tree")

Built-in constructions include: inscribed right triangle (Thales), right-triangle squares (Pythagoras), xy axes, number line, bell curve, unit-circle angle, flow boxes, and a tree layout.

60.html:
The library is a flywheel, not a fixed set. When Woopy builds a good, reusable construction, it can save it:

draw_lib_add(
  name:     "benzene_ring",
  tags:     "chemistry,hexagon,aromatic",
  template: "[DEF:benzene:cx,cy,r] … [ENDDEF]"
)

The construction is written to data/woopy-draw-library.json and merged into future draw_lib searches. So a figure Woopy gets right once becomes a reusable word in the language — and Woodr's vocabulary grows the more it's used.

62.html: Marks are the things Woodr actually draws. Everything higher-level (relational points, iteration, macros) ultimately compiles to these. Coordinates are pixels on the active screen; any coordinate can be a @NAME reference.

63.html:
MarkDraws
[POINT:x,y:label]A dot with a short label
[LINE:x1,y1,x2,y2:label]A straight line (the :label is optional)
[ARROW:x1,y1,x2,y2:label]An arrow from p1 → p2
[BOX:x,y,w,h:label]A rectangle (top-left origin)
[ELLIPSE:cx,cy,rx,ry:label]A real circle/ellipse (rx = ry → circle)
[CURVE:x1,y1;x2,y2;…:label]A smooth curve through the points
[POLY:x1,y1;x2,y2;…:label]A closed polygon
[SQUARE:x1,y1,x2,y2,awayX,awayY:label]A square on side p1–p2, built on the side away from the given interior point

[LINE] and [ARROW] separate coordinates with commas. Only the point-list marks ([CURVE], [POLY], [CONNECT]) use semicolons between points.

66.html:
To mark actual text on the screen (a word, a line of code, an error), don't box a guessed rectangle — name the text and Woodr finds it by OCR:

[HIGHLIGHT:"deprecated"]     [UNDERLINE:"submit"]
[CIRCLE:"error"]             [STRIKE:"old value"]

Add @x,y after the quote to disambiguate a repeated phrase.

67.title: Attention & motion

68.html:
The core explanatory gesture (the same idea as Manim's Indicate): the target briefly grows past its size and flashes a warm colour, then settles back. One shot — it draws the eye without the nagging of a forever [PULSE].

[INDICATE:@P:the vertex]              ; point form — grows a ring in at a spot
[INDICATE:640,300,360,120:this term]  ; region form — grows a frame around a box

Reach for it whenever you say "notice this" / "here's the key part" — a vertex, a term in an equation, a box in a diagram, a control on screen. It's the difference between a static drawing and one that directs attention over time.

CueUse when
[INDICATE]Draw the eye to one thing once, then move on (the default).
[PULSE]Something must stay flagged the whole time (a live warning).
[SPOTLIGHT]Everything else should recede — isolate one region completely.
[RIPPLE]Show where an action happens (a tap/click point).

70.html:
Choreography (see Choreography) reveals marks step by step as you speak. Motion is different: it makes a mark move continuously over a span of seconds. This is what puts Woodr in Manim's space — but live, spoken, and on your real screen.

The idea is stolen straight from GeoGebra's sliders: an animated value is just a free variable; sweeping it re-drives everything defined in terms of it. Woodr already resolves a scene from its relationships, so to animate, it simply re-resolves the whole scene each frame with the swept value substituted in. The resolver is the animation engine.

71.html:
[ANIM:t: from to dur=Xs ease=inout]
   … your scene, using t …
[ENDANIM]

t sweeps from from to to over dur seconds; every frame the scene is redrawn with the current t. ease is inout (default), linear, in, or out. Add loop to repeat.

Anything defined before the block is available inside it, but keep the animated scene inside the block — that's what gets redrawn.

72.html:
[PT:A:200,400][PT:B:900,400]
[ANIM:t:0 1 dur=2s]
  [PT:P:along A B t][POINT:@P:moving]
[ENDANIM]

P is along A B t; as t goes 0 → 1, P slides from A to B.

72.title: Glide a point along a segment

73.html:
The canonical calculus animation, and the reason Motion matters:

[ANIM:s:0.3 4.7 dur=4s]
  [PLOT:f:0.6*x^2-0.1*x^3:0,5,300,200,900,500]
  [PT:C:onplot f s]
  [COLOR:red][TANLINE:f:s]
  [COLOR:blue][POINT:@C:here]
[ENDANIM]

As s sweeps the domain, the contact point rides the curve and the tangent line pivots with the true local slope — you watch the derivative change. Nothing about the tangent is animated by hand; it re-resolves exactly, every frame.

73.title: The derivative — a tangent sliding along a curve

74.title: Orbit a point around a circle

75.html:
To show both the mover and the path it sweeps, draw the path statically with a [PCURVE] and move a point along it:

[PCURVE:S: 640+3*a*cos(a) ; 360+3*a*sin(a) ; a 0 25 : spiral]
[ANIM:t:0 1 dur=3s]
  [PT:P:pointon S t][POINT:@P:tracing]
[ENDANIM]

Reach for Motion when change over time is the point — a sweep, an orbit, a growing angle, a derivative. For a static figure revealed in sync with your words, use plain choreography instead. One animation per turn; keep the scene small.

76.html: At compile time the [ANIM]…[ENDANIM] block is lifted out, the variable is swept across ~25 frames per second, and each frame is fully re-resolved to exact marks and stored. The renderer plays the frames on a timer in a dedicated layer, then holds the final frame. Deterministic, self-contained, and it reuses the exact same drawing path as static marks — so an animated tangent looks identical to a still one.

77.html: [CURVE] (see Marks) smooths through raw coordinates. [PATH] and [PCURVE] are the relational, registered upgrades: they take named points or formulas, they can be closed and tensioned, and — crucially — you can put points on them.
77.text:
[CURVE] (see Marks) smooths through raw coordinates. [PATH] and
[PCURVE] are the relational, registered upgrades: they take named points or formulas,
they can be closed and tensioned, and — crucially — you can put points on them.
77.title: Paths & parametric curves

78.html:
[PATH:NAME: A .. B .. C .. D]

Draws a smooth curve through the named knots A, B, C, D (a centripetal Catmull-Rom spline — it passes through every knot exactly, with no overshoot). Options:

  • .. cycle closes the curve into a loop.
  • tension 0.4 tightens it toward straight segments (0 = full curve, 1 = polyline).
  • : label at the end names it on screen.
[PT:A:200,300][PT:B:500,180][PT:C:800,320][PT:D:1100,240]
[PATH:river: A .. B .. C .. D : the path]

[PT:P:120,500][PT:Q:520,520][PT:R:320,760]
[PATH:blob: P .. Q .. R .. cycle tension 0.3]
78.text:
[PATH:NAME: A .. B .. C .. D]

Draws a smooth curve through the named knots A, B, C, D (a centripetal Catmull-Rom spline —
it passes through every knot exactly, with no overshoot). Options:

.. cycle closes the curve into a loop.
tension 0.4 tightens it toward straight segments (0 = full curve, 1 = polyline).
: label at the end names it on screen.

[PT:A:200,300][PT:B:500,180][PT:C:800,320][PT:D:1100,240]
[PATH:river: A .. B .. C .. D : the path]

[PT:P:120,500][PT:Q:520,520][PT:R:320,760]
[PATH:blob: P .. Q .. R .. cycle tension 0.3]
78.title: [PATH] — a smooth curve through named points

79.html:
[PCURVE:NAME: xexpr ; yexpr ; t0 t1 : label]

Plots (x(t), y(t)) as t runs from t0 to t1 — the things y = f(x) can't draw: circles, spirals, Lissajous figures, cycloids. The formulas take the same functions as [PLOT] and must use parentheses: cos(t), not cos t.

[PCURVE:orbit: 640+200*cos(t) ; 360+200*sin(t) ; t 0 6.283 : circle]
[PCURVE:spiral: 640+3*t*cos(t) ; 360+3*t*sin(t) ; t 0 25 : spiral]
[PCURVE:liss: 640+300*sin(3*t) ; 360+300*sin(2*t) ; t 0 6.283]

80.html:
Once a [PATH] or [PCURVE] is registered, points can sit on it:

PointMeaning
[PT:G:pointon NAME t]The point at arc-fraction t (0..1) along the curve — even-speed, so it's ideal to animate
[PT:F:closest P on NAME]The nearest point on the curve to P

closest … on also works on a circle or a plotted function — it's the general foot-of-perpendicular onto any curve:

[CIRCLE:O:640,360,200][PT:P:1000,360]
[PT:F:closest P on O][POINT:@F:nearest point on the circle]

Combine the two: draw the trail with [PCURVE], then move a pointon it with [ANIM] — the mover and its path from one construction. See Motion.

91.html:
Woodr compiles in this order, then the plain marks are drawn:

  1. [ANIM]…[ENDANIM] — lifted to an animation marker, its scene stashed for per-frame re-resolution
  2. [DEF]/[USE] — expand macros (params substituted, locals namespaced)
  3. [IF] — resolve conditionals
  4. [REPEAT] — expand loops
  5. [GROUP]…[ENDGROUP] — the inner scene resolved in isolation, then translated/scaled as a unit
  6. Numeric figures — [VFIELD] [NUMLINE] [IMPLICIT] [MORPH] [GRIDXFORM] [AXES] [BARS] [SCATTER]
  7. [PLOT] → a drawn [CURVE] + registered so onplot/tanpoint/[TANLINE] work
  8. [PT]/[CIRCLE]/[PATH]/[PCURVE] — resolve relational points, circles & curves (in text order)
  9. [PATH]/[PCURVE] → dense [CURVE]; [BISECT]/[TANLINE]/[AREA] → lines/regions
  10. @@NAME → family point-lists, @NAME → coordinates
  11. [CIRCLE] → [ELLIPSE], [RIGHTANGLE] → [POLY], then [ANGLEARC]/[DIM] (post-@ numeric)

Names may contain underscores ([A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_]*) — macro locals are namespaced to u1_NAME and resolve like any other name.

Each animation frame runs this same pipeline with the swept variable substituted in. Marks are finally parsed in document order, so the [COLOR]/[THEME] pen applies to exactly the marks that follow it.
